question: A finite block-encoding candidate stores a target operator A on the system register, a scalar normalizer alpha, a register layout, and one large unitary U that also acts on signal and pure-ancilla qubits. State precisely which submatrix of U is claimed to reproduce A, how the normalizer enters, and what the exact-versus-approximate contract is. If U acts on n system qubits and a auxiliary qubits, what is the dimension of U and of the extracted block, and what single scalar equation must the extracted entries satisfy in the exact case?
reference_answer: The candidate claims that the projected block obtained by sandwiching U between the all-zero auxiliary bra and ket, (<0^a| tensor I) U (|0^a> tensor I), equals A up to the normalizer. In the exact case A = alpha * (<0^a| tensor I) U (|0^a> tensor I) entrywise; equivalently the projected block equals A/alpha. In the approximate case the contract is the operator-norm inequality ||A - alpha * (<0^a| tensor I) U (|0^a> tensor I)|| <= epsilon, and the exact case is recovered at epsilon = 0. Dimensions: with N = 2^n system dimensions and a auxiliary qubits, U is a 2^(n+a) x 2^(n+a) unitary and the extracted block is the N x N submatrix indexed by auxiliary value 0 on both sides. The per-entry scalar requirement in the exact case is block(i,j) = A(i,j)/alpha, i.e. the entry of U at compound row (auxiliary 0, system i) and compound column (auxiliary 0, system j) equals A(i,j)/alpha. The normalizer is a stored contract scalar, not asserted optimal.

State the exact entrywise relation A = alpha*block (block = A/alpha) and the approximate operator-norm bound with epsilon=0 as the exact case
Give correct dimensions 2^(n+a) for U and 2^n for the block, and the per-entry scalar equation

alpha is a stored normalizer scalar, not asserted optimal
conventions: Auxiliary register pinned to the all-zero value selects the clean block
Exact case is the epsilon=0 instance of the approximate operator-norm bound

The exact contract A = alpha*block is the epsilon=0 case of the stored operator-norm approximation bound.

question: The register layout of a block-encoding candidate separates signal qubits from pure ancilla qubits, and the auxiliary count used by the cost score adds them together. Explain the distinct semantic role of the two kinds of auxiliary qubit, why both are charged in the auxiliary total, and what postselection or cleanliness assumption each imposes on a valid certificate. Is a pure ancilla allowed to be left in an arbitrary state at the output of the clean branch?
reference_answer: Signal qubits are the register whose all-zero value selects the encoded block: the block encoding is read by projecting onto signal value 0, so signal qubits carry the postselection/flag that must succeed. Pure ancilla qubits are working qubits that the construction borrows and must return to the all-zero state at the end of the clean branch; they are not a selection flag but they still enlarge the unitary. The auxiliary total adds signalQubits + pureAncillas because the Hilbert-space blow-up and the clean-projection constraint depend on both: the extracted block is indexed by the all-zero value of the entire auxiliary register (signal and pure ancilla together). A pure ancilla may NOT be left in an arbitrary state on the clean branch: the block-correctness contract uses the all-zero auxiliary bra and ket on both sides, so any residual ancilla excitation on the clean output would move amplitude out of the projected block and break the exact (or epsilon) equality. The distinction is a cleanliness assumption (pure ancillas returned to zero) plus a selection assumption (signal projected to zero), and both are charged.

Describe pure ancillas as borrowed working qubits that must be returned to zero on the clean branch
Explain auxiliary total = signal + pure ancilla because the clean projection pins the whole auxiliary register to zero, and that an uncleaned ancilla breaks block correctness

conventions: auxiliaryQubits = signalQubits + pureAncillas
Clean block uses the all-zero auxiliary bra and ket simultaneously

A residual pure-ancilla excitation on the clean branch leaves the projected block, breaking block correctness.

question: Fix a total space of dimension 2 and a system embedding that sends the single system index to total index 0, so the clean block is the one entry U(0,0). A contributor claims that specifying the target A (here the scalar at position (0,0)) and demanding U be real orthogonal determines U uniquely. Refute this: for the target entry x with 0 < |x| < 1, exhibit two DISTINCT real orthogonal 2x2 matrices whose clean block is the same x, verify both are orthogonal, identify exactly which matrix data is left free by the block-encoding contract, and state the general principle about how much of U a clean-block (or even clean-action) certificate pins down.
reference_answer: The clean block under this embedding is the single entry U(0,0); the contract only requires U(0,0) = x (times the normalizer, here 1) and U real orthogonal. Two distinct witnesses with x in (0,1), set s = sqrt(1-x^2) > 0: U1 = [[x, -s],[s, x]] (a proper rotation) and U2 = [[x, s],[s, -x]] (a reflection). Both have clean block U1(0,0) = U2(0,0) = x. Orthogonality: U1 columns have squared norms x^2+s^2 = 1 and x^2+s^2 = 1 with cross term x*(-s)+s*x = 0; U2 columns have x^2+s^2 = 1 and s^2+x^2 = 1 with cross term x*s + s*(-x) = 0. So both are orthogonal, and U1 != U2 because their (0,1) entries are -s and s and their (1,1) entries are x and -x (and s > 0). Hence the target entry plus orthogonality does NOT determine U: the block-encoding contract constrains only the clean (embedded) rows and columns, and everything off that clean embedding - the 'garbage' or failure branch - is free, subject only to making the whole matrix orthogonal. General principle: a clean-block certificate fixes U exactly on the clean sub-block (the all-zero-ancilla rows and columns); the orthogonal complement (the nonzero-ancilla branch) is determined only up to any completion to a unitary, so infinitely many distinct U (for larger blocks) share the same block encoding of A. Even the stronger clean-ACTION certificate (U on every clean basis input, read on clean outputs) pins only the clean block and the same freedom remains, because that action and the clean block carry identical information. The practical consequence: you cannot read U, its depth, or its ancilla content off A alone; distinct constructions with very different costs can encode the same A, which is exactly why the benchmark certifies clean blocks and charges resources separately rather than treating the dilating unitary as unique.

Identify the free data as the off-clean-embedding entries (garbage/failure branch), constrained only by overall orthogonality
State the general principle: a clean-block (or clean-action) certificate pins U only on the clean sub-block; the completion is non-unique, so A does not determine U or its cost

Clean block is the single embedded entry U(0,0)
conventions: cleanBlockBy embed U (row,col) = U(embed row, embed col); here embed sends the system index to total index 0

question: A logical linear-combination-of-unitaries block encoding is assembled as unprepare after select after amplitude after prepare, on a product of a coefficient register, a selector register, and the system register. Describe the role of each of the four stages, say which registers each stage touches, and explain why the final stage is the adjoint (dagger) of the first rather than an independent gate. What exactly plays the role of the ancilla that must be returned to zero?
reference_answer: PREPARE acts on the selector register (lifted by tensoring with identities on the coefficient and system registers): it loads the superposition of selector values whose amplitudes encode the LCU weights. AMPLITUDE is a selector- and system-controlled family of unitaries acting on the coefficient register (block-diagonal over the (selector,system) context): it writes the per-term coefficient/rotation into the coefficient register. SELECT is a basis permutation that applies, controlled by the selector value, the chosen system permutation to the system register while preserving coefficient and selector: it applies the term unitaries to the data. UNPREPARE is the adjoint of PREPARE on the selector register; it must be the dagger of the first stage because the clean block is read by projecting the selector (and coefficient) back onto the clean value, and only PREPARE-dagger coherently recombines the selector superposition so the surviving clean amplitude is the weighted sum of term contributions. An independent gate would not guarantee that the clean projection reconstructs the intended weights or returns the selector to zero. The ancilla that must return to zero is the selector register (together with the coefficient register pinned to its clean value); PREPARE and UNPREPARE act on this SAME selector register, which is what produces the weight structure in the clean entry.

Assign SELECT to the controlled system permutation preserving coefficient and selector
Explain why UNPREPARE is PREPARE-dagger on the SAME selector register and that the selector/coefficient clean value is the ancilla returned to zero

question: Fix the clean signal value. Prove that the following two certificate conditions are equivalent: (i) the projected system x system block of U equals a target A entrywise; (ii) for every system basis input and output, the clean output amplitude of U on the clean basis input (clean signal, basis input) equals A(output,input). Explain each direction, name the single linear-algebra fact that makes one clean-basis amplitude equal to one projected-block entry, and state how (ii) extends from basis inputs to an arbitrary normalized system input.
reference_answer: Write the compound (flattened) index for signal value s and system index k as s*systemDim + k, with s fixed to the clean value throughout. The projected block entry at (output,input) is block(output,input) = U(clean*systemDim+output, clean*systemDim+input). The clean output amplitude is the coordinate at compound index (clean,output) of the vector U applied to the basis ket at compound index (clean,input). Key fact: applying a matrix to a computational basis ket selects the corresponding column of the matrix (mulVec of a single-one indicator yields that column). Hence the clean output amplitude equals U(clean*systemDim+output, clean*systemDim+input), which is exactly block(output,input). (i) => (ii): if block = A entrywise, then for each (output,input) the clean output amplitude equals block(output,input) = A(output,input). (ii) => (i): if every clean output amplitude equals A(output,input), then by the same column-selection identity every projected-block entry equals A(output,input), so block = A entrywise. The two statements are therefore pointwise equivalent at the fixed signal value. Extension to arbitrary input: write a normalized system state as a linear combination of system basis vectors; the clean output on this input is the same linear combination of the per-basis clean outputs by linearity of matrix-vector action, so the clean-branch action equals A acting on the system state (up to the normalizer and the orthogonal failure branch, which only records the unitarity probability deficit). This equivalence is why a construction may prove the block directly or prove the clean action and conclude the other.

rubric.criterion: Identify the column-selection fact (matrix applied to a basis ket = that column) as the bridge, and show one clean-basis amplitude equals one projected-block entry via the compound index s*systemDim+k
Prove both directions (i)=>(ii) and (ii)=>(i) pointwise at the fixed signal value
Extend (ii) from basis inputs to an arbitrary normalized input by linearity, noting the normalizer and that the failure branch is only unitarity evidence

question: For the logical unprepare-select-amplitude-prepare LCU matrix on registers coefficient x (selector x system), derive the exact clean projected entry between clean input (clean coefficient, clean selector, systemColumn) and clean output (clean coefficient, clean selector, systemRow). Show that it is a finite sum over selector indices, that each surviving term carries the SELECT matching condition on the system permutation, and that each term's weight is the conjugate of a PREPARE amplitude times the controlled coefficient rotation diagonal entry times the PREPARE amplitude. Explain concretely why the selector weight appears as conjugate-times-itself and what this means physically.
reference_answer: Project the logical matrix onto the clean coefficient and clean selector on both sides, leaving system indices systemRow (output) and systemColumn (input). The clean entry equals the finite sum over all selector indices j of: [if permutation(j) applied to systemColumn equals systemRow then conj(prepare(j, cleanSelector)) * rotation(j, systemColumn)(cleanCoefficient, cleanCoefficient) * prepare(j, cleanSelector) else 0]. Derivation: UNPREPARE = PREPARE-dagger lifted on the selector contributes the clean bra, which turns the matrix product into a selector sum against conj(prepare(j, cleanSelector)) and forces the coefficient and system row labels; AMPLITUDE contributes the controlled coefficient-register entry rotation(j, systemColumn)(cleanCoefficient, cleanCoefficient) on the clean coefficient diagonal; SELECT contributes the indicator that the controlled system permutation for selector j maps the input systemColumn to the output systemRow; PREPARE contributes the ket amplitude prepare(j, cleanSelector). The selector weight is conj(prepare(j,cleanSelector)) * (...) * prepare(j,cleanSelector): the factor prepare(j,cleanSelector) comes from PREPARE loading the selector superposition from the clean selector, and the factor conj(prepare(j,cleanSelector)) comes from UNPREPARE = PREPARE-dagger projecting back onto the clean selector. Physically this is why PREPARE and UNPREPARE must be the SAME gate up to adjoint acting on the SAME selector register: the clean amplitude of each term is weighted by |prepare(j,cleanSelector)|^2 when the coefficient rotation diagonal is 1, i.e. by the probability of selecting term j, so the clean block is the probability-weighted (and coefficient-weighted) combination of the per-term system permutations. If prepare and unprepare were independent, the two factors would not form conj(x)*x and the clean weights would not be the intended squared selection amplitudes.

question: A block encoding is read by preparing the auxiliary register in the all-zero state, applying U, and postselecting the auxiliary register back on all-zero. Suppose U block-encodes A with normalizer alpha (so the auxiliary-zero projected block equals A/alpha) and the input system state is a normalized vector v. Express the unnormalized clean output branch and its squared norm, give the exact success probability of the all-zero postselection, and state when this probability equals (||A v|| / alpha)^2. Why is the success probability generally strictly below 1, and what does this cost imply for using the block encoding as a subroutine?
reference_answer: Prepare |0^a> tensor |v>, apply U. Decompose the output as |0^a> tensor w_clean + (orthogonal auxiliary-nonzero branches), where w_clean = (<0^a| tensor I) U (|0^a> tensor |v>). Because the auxiliary-zero projected block of U equals A/alpha, w_clean = (A/alpha) v. The all-zero postselection keeps exactly the clean branch, so the unnormalized clean output is (A/alpha) v with squared norm ||(A/alpha) v||^2 = ||A v||^2 / alpha^2, and the post-measurement normalized state is (A v)/||A v||. The success probability of the all-zero auxiliary outcome is therefore p = ||A v||^2 / alpha^2 = (||A v|| / alpha)^2. This equals (||A v||/alpha)^2 exactly whenever the projected block is exactly A/alpha (the exact block-encoding case); in the epsilon-approximate case it is this value up to an O(epsilon) correction. Since U is unitary, the total output norm is 1, so p <= 1 with equality only in the degenerate case ||A v|| = alpha (e.g. alpha = ||A|| and v a top singular vector with the orthogonal branch empty); generically ||A v|| < alpha (alpha is chosen at least the operator norm so the encoding is valid for all v), so p < 1 strictly. The cost implication: one query to U succeeds with probability p that can be far below 1, so naive repetition costs O(1/p) = O(alpha^2/||A v||^2) trials; amplitude amplification reduces this to O(alpha/||A v||) queries. This 1/alpha success penalty is exactly why the normalizer alpha is a charged resource and why alpha should be kept close to ||A||.

question: Consider the 2x2 scalar dilation whose top-left clean entry is x, whose two off-diagonal entries are both y, and whose bottom-right entry is -x. Treat the single top-left entry as the one-dimensional clean block encoding the scalar x with normalizer 1. Determine the exact condition on (x,y) under which this dilation is orthogonal (a valid real one-qubit-signal block encoding), compute the two row self-overlaps and the row cross-overlap, and explain the boundary: what is the largest |x| for which a real y exists making the dilation orthogonal, and what does exceeding it mean for block-encoding a scalar of magnitude greater than 1 with normalizer 1?
reference_answer: The dilation matrix is [[x, y],[y, -x]]. Its row self-overlaps are: row 0 with itself = x*x + y*y, row 1 with itself = (-x)*(-x) + y*y = x*x + y*y, and the row cross-overlap (row 0 with row 1) = x*y + y*(-x) = x*y - x*y = 0. So the rows are automatically orthogonal to each other for all (x,y), and the matrix is orthogonal (a valid real block encoding whose clean block is the scalar x) exactly when the common self-overlap equals 1, i.e. x*x + y*y = 1. Given x, a real y with y*y = 1 - x*x exists iff 1 - x*x >= 0, i.e. |x| <= 1; then y = +/- sqrt(1 - x^2). The largest |x| admitting a real y is therefore |x| = 1 (at which y = 0 and the dilation is diag(1,-1) up to sign). Boundary meaning: a 1x1 clean block with normalizer 1 can only encode a scalar of magnitude at most 1; this is the contraction constraint, since the clean block of any unitary (or orthogonal) matrix is a contraction with operator norm at most 1. To block-encode a scalar c with |c| > 1 one must either raise the normalizer to alpha >= |c| (encoding c/alpha, which again has magnitude <= 1) or use a larger signal register; no choice of real y rescues |x| > 1. Thus the scalar-dilation gives the sharp one-dimensional instance of the general lower bound: the encoded block, before dividing by the normalizer, cannot have norm exceeding 1.

question: A one-sparse block-encoding route reconstructs a target matrix from a column support map c and column amplitudes: entry (row, col) is amp(col) when row = c(col) and 0 otherwise. Suppose a contributor claims this route can exactly encode ANY matrix with at most one nonzero per column. Give a concrete small target that is NOT reconstructed by the one-sparse formula, state exactly which hypothesis of the one-sparse reconstruction lemma it violates, and then exhibit a genuine zero-containing one-sparse target that IS correctly reconstructed, confirming that a zero amplitude column is allowed but a second nonzero per column is not.
reference_answer: The one-sparse model is: oneSparseMatrix c amp has entry (row,col) = amp(col) if row = c(col), else 0 - so each column has its single possible nonzero at the single row c(col). The reconstruction lemma assumes the target is supported only at row = c(col), i.e. for all row != c(col), target(row,col) = 0 (one nonzero per column at a FIXED location). Counterexample to the overbroad claim: take the 2x2 target A with A(0,0)=1, A(1,0)=1, and column 1 all zero. Column 0 has TWO nonzeros (rows 0 and 1), so there is no single support value c(0) with target(row,0)=0 for all row != c(0): whichever of row 0 or 1 we pick as c(0), the other row is a nonzero off-support entry. Hence the support hypothesis fails and oneSparseMatrix c (fun col => A (c col) col) cannot equal A for any c: it would zero out one of the two entries. The violated hypothesis is precisely 'row != c(col) implies target(row,col)=0'. Now a genuine zero-containing one-sparse target that IS reconstructed: take B 2x2 with B(0,0)=0 (column 0 entirely zero) and B(1,1)=3 (column 1 nonzero at row 1), all other entries 0. Choose c(0)=0 and c(1)=1. For column 0, amp(0)=B(c(0),0)=B(0,0)=0, and every entry is 0, matching B; the zero amplitude is allowed. For column 1, amp(1)=B(1,1)=3 at row 1 and 0 elsewhere, matching B. So oneSparseMatrix c amp = B exactly. Conclusion: one nonzero per column at a fixed support location (including the degenerate zero-amplitude column) is fine; TWO nonzeros in a column breaks the sole hypothesis and is a true counterexample to the overbroad claim.

question: To block-encode a product A*B from a block encoding of A and a block encoding of B, the product clean block is formed as the matrix product of the two clean blocks. A contributor argues: since both factors use an all-zero ancilla and project back to all-zero, we can reuse the SAME physical ancilla register for both factors and still get the product clean block. Explain why the correct composition requires each factor's clean block to be extracted independently, give the precise algebraic statement that is actually proved (which operation on clean blocks is used and under which congruence), and then explain the flaw in the same-ancilla argument by describing the intermediate state that a shared ancilla cannot represent. Does the proved product leaf itself charge any ancilla reuse?
reference_answer: What is actually proved: if left and right are two certificates whose clean blocks equal their targets pointwise (left.cleanBlock = left.target and right.cleanBlock = right.target), then the product certificate has clean block = matrix-product(left.cleanBlock, right.cleanBlock) and target = matrix-product(left.target, right.target), and the block proof is the congruence 'pointwise equality is preserved under matrix multiplication' (by entrywise substitution in the finite product sum): from left.cleanBlock = left.target and right.cleanBlock = right.target one concludes product(left.cleanBlock,right.cleanBlock) = product(left.target,right.target). Crucially this is an identity about the two ALREADY-EXTRACTED clean blocks: each clean block is the all-zero-ancilla projection of its own unitary, computed independently, and only then are the two system-space matrices multiplied. Why the same-ancilla argument is flawed: physically the product unitary applies U_B first, then U_A, to the system register. After U_B the ancilla is returned to all-zero ONLY on the clean branch; the full state is |0^a> tensor (B/alphaB) v + (orthogonal ancilla-nonzero garbage). To feed U_A correctly, U_A needs its ancilla freshly in all-zero. If U_A reuses the SAME physical register that U_B left, then on the ancilla-nonzero garbage branch U_A acts on a nonzero ancilla value and its output does not correspond to the clean projection of U_A at all; the clean branch of the composite is no longer the clean block of A applied to the clean block of B unless the ancilla has been reset to all-zero (a fresh/cleaned register) before U_A. The matrix-product-of-clean-blocks identity silently assumes exactly this independent clean extraction. So a correct product needs each factor to see an all-zero ancilla - either disjoint ancilla registers (product resource cost adds the auxiliary counts) or an explicit uncompute/reset between factors; sharing the register without resetting conflates the clean branch with the garbage branch. The proved product leaf itself is pure clean-block matrix algebra and does NOT model or charge ancilla reuse; the resource side is handled separately, where the product-style resource cost ADDS the auxiliary qubits of the two factors, reflecting that the clean composition is not free in ancillas.

question: In an LCU-style assembly of a Hermitian piece, each selected term contributes a scaled controlled-phase source whose upper block carries the intended operator and whose lower-right filler block is normalizer times a phase e^{i*phi}. A source writes both filler phases as e^{i*pi} = -1 and claims the two filler blocks cancel so the clean block equals the intended Hermitian piece S1. Show by direct computation of the lower-right clean entry that the printed all-(-1)-phase choice does NOT cancel, give the exact value of that entry, prove the clean block therefore differs from S1 when the normalizer is nonzero, and exhibit the corrected phase assignment that does make the fillers cancel while preserving the intended operator blocks.
reference_answer: The assembly adds three scaled sources (each scaled by 1/2): a controlled-phase source for A with filler phase, one for A-dagger with filler phase, and a Pauli-X-tensor-B term that has zero lower-right block. The lower-right filler of a scaled controlled-phase source with normalizer N and phase e^{i*phi} is (1/2)*N*e^{i*phi} on the diagonal. With BOTH A and A-dagger terms using phase e^{i*pi} = -1, the lower-right diagonal clean entry is (1/2)*N*(-1) + (1/2)*N*(-1) + 0 = -N. So the printed clean lower-right block equals -N (the identity-filler blocks ADD rather than cancel). But the intended Hermitian piece S1 has lower-right block equal to 0 (S1 is the Hermitian part of the homogenized matrix [[A,B],[0,0]], whose lower-right block is 0). Therefore, if N != 0, the printed clean block has lower-right entry -N != 0 = S1's lower-right entry, so the printed-phase clean block is NOT equal to S1 - a genuine counterexample to the all-(-1) cancellation claim. Corrected assignment: give the two filler phases OPPOSITE signs, e.g. keep the A-dagger term at phase -1 but set the A term's filler phase to 0 (i.e. e^{i*0}=+1) while leaving its upper operator block intact. Then the lower-right clean entry becomes (1/2)*N*(+1) + (1/2)*N*(-1) + 0 = 0, matching S1's zero lower-right block, and the upper A, A-dagger and off-diagonal B blocks are unchanged, so the phase-balanced clean block equals S1 exactly (under the paper's Hermitian B). The lesson: filler phases are a real proof obligation - identical phases add, opposite phases cancel; only a phase-balanced choice recovers the intended block.

Show S1's lower-right block is 0, hence for N!=0 the printed clean block differs from S1 (genuine counterexample)
Give the corrected opposite/phase-balanced assignment making the lower-right entry 0 while preserving upper operator blocks, so the clean block equals S1

question: A reversible-classical block-encoding route realizes the full unitary as a permutation matrix on the flattened ancilla-system basis, with the clean block taken from the all-zero ancilla embedding. Prove that a permutation matrix built from a bijective index map is a valid real orthogonal unitary proxy (its column and row Gram matrices are the identity), and separately give the exact clean-block entry formula for such a permutation under the product embedding. Explain why bijectivity (not merely injectivity) is needed for the row Gram condition, and why the clean block of a permutation is itself a 0/1 partial-permutation matrix rather than an arbitrary target.
reference_answer: A permutation matrix for an index map p has entry (row,col) = 1 if row = p(col) else 0. Column Gram: columnInner(i,j) = sum over k of permMatrix(k,i)*permMatrix(k,j). The product permMatrix(k,i)*permMatrix(k,j) is nonzero only when k = p(i) and k = p(j) simultaneously. If i = j the unique surviving term is at k = p(i) giving 1; if i != j then p(i) != p(j) by INJECTIVITY, so no k satisfies both and the sum is 0. Hence columnInner = identity using only injectivity. Row Gram: rowInner(i,j) = sum over k of permMatrix(i,k)*permMatrix(j,k), nonzero only when i = p(k) and j = p(k). For the diagonal i = j we need SOME k with p(k) = i, i.e. i is in the image of p; this requires SURJECTIVITY. With bijectivity, for each i there is exactly one such k (hit = p^{-1}(i)) giving 1, and for i != j no k maps to both, giving 0, so rowInner = identity. Thus bijectivity (injective AND surjective) yields IsRationalOrthogonal(permMatrix p): injectivity alone secures the column condition, but the row (diagonal) condition can fail without surjectivity because some row might have no preimage and give rowInner(i,i)=0 != 1. Clean block entry: under the product embedding productIndex (ancilla, system) mapping (a,s) to a*system + s, the clean block uses the all-zero ancilla embedding, and cleanBlockProduct(zero, permMatrix p)(row,col) = 1 if productIndex(zero,row) = p(productIndex(zero,col)) else 0. This is manifestly a 0/1 matrix with at most one 1 per column (a partial permutation of the system basis): it can only equal targets that are themselves 0/1 partial permutations, so a permutation-matrix block encoding cannot directly encode a target with non-0/1 entries - that needs weighting/LCU layers on top. The reversible-classical route therefore certifies exactly the partial-permutation clean blocks and no more.

rubric.criterion: Prove columnInner = identity using injectivity (unique surviving diagonal term, no off-diagonal term since p(i)!=p(j))

Prove rowInner = identity requires surjectivity (existence of a preimage for the diagonal), hence bijectivity gives IsRationalOrthogonal, and explain why injectivity alone is insufficient for the row condition

Give the clean-block entry formula cleanBlockProduct(zero,permMatrix p)(row,col)=1 iff productIndex(zero,row)=p(productIndex(zero,col)), and explain it is a 0/1 partial permutation that cannot encode non-0/1 targets

question: An exact clean-block certificate can be promoted to a zero-error approximate incumbent in the adaptive exact-to-approximate search policy. State what data an exact clean-block certificate carries, what the zero-error promotion sets the epsilon and the approximation predicate to, and why an exact certificate is a legitimate epsilon=0 member of the approximate search without any additional analytic norm argument. Then explain the boundary the other way: does holding a zero-error approximate incumbent let you conclude an operator-norm bound ||A - alpha*block|| <= 0, and if not, what extra ingredient is required?
reference_answer: An exact clean-block certificate carries: a full matrix U on the total (ancilla+system) basis, a target system-space matrix A, an embedding of the system basis into the total basis, and a proof that the embedded clean block of U equals A pointwise (the clean submatrix equals A entry by entry). The zero-error promotion sets epsilon = 0 and sets the approximation predicate to be exactly that same pointwise clean-block equality, with the approximation proof being the certificate's own block proof. This is legitimate because the approximate incumbent's bound field is a PROPOSITION that different backends may instantiate; the exact finite route instantiates the epsilon=0 bound by the exact pointwise equality it already proved, so no analytic operator-norm reasoning is introduced - the promotion is a repackaging, not a new theorem. Boundary the other way: holding this zero-error approximate incumbent does NOT by itself yield the analytic statement ||A - alpha*block|| <= 0 in an operator-norm sense. The finite certificate proves ENTRYWISE (pointwise) equality of the clean block with A/normalizer; converting that to an operator-norm inequality (or to the statement that the operator-norm distance is 0) requires the extra ingredient of a theorem connecting pointwise/entrywise equality of finite matrices to the chosen matrix norm (e.g. that pointwise equality implies equality as operators and hence zero norm difference). The source is explicit that analytic backends can LATER replace the exact-as-approximate packaging with such a theorem; until then the epsilon=0 incumbent is a faithful exact-equality witness, not an analytic norm certificate. So the exact-to-approximate direction is free (repackaging), but the approximate-norm interpretation needs an added norm-vs-pointwise bridge.
